content: 1. The research questions focus on the effects of various caregiving interventions on early childhood development (ECD) during the first three years of life. These include responsive caregiving interventions, interventions promoting early learning, and combined approaches that integrate both responsive caregiving and early learning promotion. 2. The systematic reviews adhered to a common set of inclusion and exclusion criteria across all PICO questions, with specific criteria tailored to each question. There were no temporal or regional constraints imposed on the studies. 3. Inclusion criteria required primary studies published in peer-reviewed journals, interventions evaluated using randomized controlled trial (RCT) designs with at least one control and one intervention group, and interventions targeting children and their caregivers during early life (from pregnancy to three years of age). The studies had to assess at least one ECD outcome (e.g., cognition, language, motor, socioemotional development, or behavior) as a primary outcome and evaluate outcomes immediately after or shortly following the intervention. 4. Caregivers were defined as the legal guardian, biological parent, or adult responsible for the child’s well-being. Interventions targeting caregivers with illnesses or disabilities were included, while those not relevant to caregiving or not evaluated using RCT designs were excluded. 5. The literature search was conducted across five electronic bibliographic databases: EMBASE, PubMed, PsycINFO, Cochrane CENTRAL, and ERIC. Search strategies were tailored to each database, using a comprehensive string of keywords to capture caregiving interventions, early childhood age groups, RCT designs, and ECD outcomes. 6. The screening process involved initial title and abstract screening, followed by full-text review to determine eligibility. Two team members independently assessed each study to ensure accuracy, with discrepancies resolved through group discussion. Data extraction was performed using a standardized, pre-piloted form, and included details on sample characteristics, intervention characteristics, risk of bias, and data for effect size calculations. 7. Weekly in-person meetings were held to monitor progress and address discrepancies in data extraction. Quality assurance was conducted by subsampling 50% of included articles for review during the initial weeks of data extraction. 8. The risk of bias in included studies was assessed based on randomization sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and investigators, reporting of data for all participants, complete reporting of pre-specified outcomes, and other potential sources of bias (e.g., measurement reliability and validity). 9. A meta-analysis was conducted for outcomes such as ECD, child behavior, attachment, growth, nutrition, health, caregiving practices, and caregiver mental health, provided there were sufficient studies available. Standardized tools and comprehensive assessments were prioritized over non-standardized or study-specific tools. 10. A decision-making matrix was developed to address situations where multiple results for a specific outcome were reported. This approach was informed by developmental theory for language and motor development and statistical recommendations. 11. Subgroup analyses were conducted by regional context (globally, high-income countries, and lowand middle-income countries) and by intervention type. Quantitative data synthesis used fixed or random-effects meta-analysis based on heterogeneity, which was evaluated using Cochran’s Q test and the I² statistic. 12. The quality of the body of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach, categorizing evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low. GRADE evidence profiles summarized the quality and findings across studies for each critical outcome. 13. Responsive caregiving interventions were defined as those targeting the caregiver-child dyad to promote sensitive and responsive interactions, strengthen the parent-child relationship, and support secure attachment. These interventions often involved play, communication, or feeding contexts to enhance caregivers’ abilities to respond to the child’s cues and needs. 14. The review highlighted the variability in definitions of caregiving interventions in the literature, necessitating the establishment of clear definitions for each intervention type during the review process. This iterative process evolved as the team reviewed and discussed each intervention. 15. The meta-analysis results were presented using forest plots, and publication bias was assessed using the Egger regression asymmetry test. The findings were summarized in accordance with the GRADE approach, providing a comprehensive evaluation of the evidence for each research question.
